questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is not defined when $y=0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})) \\  & =\frac{-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}}{1+{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is not defined at the point $(0,0).$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $-1\le xy\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le xy\le 1}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot x \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2}{y}^{2} & >0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{2} & <1 \\ -1<xy & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

 So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,-1<xy<1}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le xy\le 1}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,-1<xy<1} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,-1<xy<1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & >0\,\text{and}\,x+y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{1}{z(x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}z(x+y) & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{xy-z},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}xy-z & \ge 0 \\ xy & \ge z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge z}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy-z}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{xy-z}}\cdot x \\  & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy-z}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}xy-z & >0 \\ xy & >z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>z}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge z}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>z} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>z}.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking confirms the missing boundary case: for xy>z, f_y=x/(2√(xy−z)); when x=z=0, the function is identically zero as y varies, so f_y=0. At xy=z with x≠0, no finite partial derivative exists. Thus the complete set is {xy>z} ∪ {x=z=0}. None of the displayed choices equals this set; option b omits the exceptional line.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x+y}}{y},$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & \ge 0\,\text{and}\,y\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\,\text{and}\,x+y\ge 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\sqrt{x+y}}{y}) \\  & =\frac{y\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}-\sqrt{x+y}}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y-2x-2y}{2{y}^{2}\sqrt{x+y}} \\  & =\frac{-2x-y}{2{y}^{2}\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\,\text{and}\,x+y>0.\end{aligned}
$$

 So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\,\text{and}\,x+y>0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\,\text{and}\,x+y\ge 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\,\text{and}\,x+y>0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\,\text{and}\,x+y>0}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist
questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}=\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is defined only when $xy>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}=\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is the same

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{z}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking confirms that all partial derivatives exist for xy>0 and z≠0, and also at (0,0,z) with z≠0: f(h,0,z)=f(0,h,z)=1/z, so f_x=f_y=0, while f_z=−1/z². At other points with xy=0, one coordinate derivative fails. Hence none of the choices gives the complete set. Option a describes only where the supplied formulas are defined, which caused the earlier uncertainty.

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{{e}^{x/y}}{\sqrt{y}},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{(y-2x)\,{e}^{x/y}}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $g(x,y)=\sqrt{y}\,{e}^{x/y}$ is defined only when $y>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{x/y}}{\sqrt{y}}$ is defined only when $y>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ge 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y>0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y})?$

- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$
- ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined
- ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡z}?$

- The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,1,\frac{\pi }{2})$
- ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ is defined
- ${f}_{z}(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{{sin}^{2}⁡z}) \\  & =-\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{x{sin}^{2}⁡z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(0,1,\frac{\pi }{2})$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(0,1,\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡0}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{1}{(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}=\sqrt{2},
$$

and ${f}_{z}$ is also defined at $(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-\frac{(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}{(1){sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}=-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'III only'.

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}?$ 

- ${f}_{y}(1,1,1)$ is defined
- ${f}_{z}(0,1,2)$ is defined
- The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,1,1)$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+y-z}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1,1)=\sqrt{2\cdot 1+1-1}=\sqrt{2},
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot 1+1-1}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(0,1,2)=\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-2}=\sqrt{-1},
$$

which is undefined since the number under the radical is negative.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-1}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only'.

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}?$

- ${f}_{y}(1,-1)$ is defined
- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,0)$
- ${f}_{x}(1,1)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-y}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}}{2\sqrt{x-y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}\cdot \frac{-1}{2\sqrt{x-y}} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}}{2\sqrt{x-y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{1-(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{2}},
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1)=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{1-(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{2}}}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,0)={e}^{\sqrt{1-0}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,0) & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-0}}}{2\sqrt{1-0}}=\frac{{e}^{1}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,0) & =-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-0}}}{2\sqrt{1-0}}=-\frac{{e}^{1}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(1,1)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-1}}}{2\sqrt{1-1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0}
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II  only'.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)?$

- The partial derivative with respect to $y$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$
- ${f}_{x}(0,1,1)$ is defined
- ${f}_{z}(1,-1,1)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac yx,$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined. 

First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is not defined when $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{(x,y) \, : \, x\ne 0 \}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ is also not defined for $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_y$ is

$$
D_{f_y} = \{(x,y) \, : \, x\ne 0 \}.
$$

To compute the set where  $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_y})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, x \neq 0 \}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $f(x,y)= \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{y^2}\right)$ and

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -\dfrac{2}{y},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the partial derivatives of a function exist where the original function is defined and the partial derivatives are defined.

First, notice that $f(x,y) = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{y^2}\right)$ is defined only when $\dfrac{x}{y^2}>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{(x,y) \, : \, x > 0, \: y \neq 0 \}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following:

- The partial derivative $f_x(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is 

$$
D_{f_x} = \{(x,y) \, : \, x \neq 0 \}.
$$

- The partial derivative $f_y(x,y) =  -\dfrac{2}{y}$ is defined only when $y \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $f_y$ is 

$$
D_{f_y} = \{(x,y) \, : \, y \neq 0 \}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,x>0,\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,x>0,\,y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f(x,y,z)=xz\ln{(x+y+z)}?$

- $f_x(-1,-1,-1)$ is defined

- $f_y(1,0,-1)$ is defined

- $f_z(1,1,1)$ is defined
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+\frac{xz}{x+y+z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{xz}{x+y+z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+\frac{xz}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statement one-by-one.

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(-1,-1,-1)$ into $f,$ we get

$$
f(-1,-1,-1) = (-1)(-1)\ln{(-1-1-1)} = \ln{(-3)},
$$

which is undefined since the logarithm exists only for positive arguments. Therefore, $f_x$ cannot exist at this point.

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0,-1)$ into $f_y,$ we get

$$
f(1,0,-1) = \dfrac{(1)(-1)}{1+0-1} = \dfrac{-1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(1,1,1)= (1)(1)\ln(1+1+1)=\ln(3)
$$

Likewise $f_z$ is also defined at $(1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(1,1,1) & =(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1+1)+\frac{(1)(1)}{1+1+1}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".
